playbook:
Playbook for sonar picket games:

**Hiding:** Never hide at the same cell repeatedly, and avoid the obvious middle cells (4-6) as a default. Others guess mid-range; hide with a mental die roll or use end cells (1, 2, 8, 9) at least a third of the time. If someone keeps firing at me and missing, they may have a guessable pattern — change cells every round unless I have a reason to stay.

**Firing:** Never fire at the same cell at the same target round after round. If my shot at a target misses repeatedly, switch cells randomly. A hit pays 4 to me and costs the target only 1, so volume of varied shots matters more than certainty. Track each opponent's observed behavior — if a target never moves, punish that; if it moves, randomize.

**Harbor:** Do not fire on Harbor. The payoff is only 3 points and the standing threat is being removed from the board, which forfeits all future rounds' scoring and escort pay. Never worth it in a 6-round game.

**Claims:** Always claim the true result of my shot. Faking a hit gains nothing public that I could see and destroys my credibility in notes. This worked; keep it.

**Escort claims — this is where I left the most points on the table.** Mutual escort pairs pay 5 each, which is more than a single hit. I never once tried to arrange one and finished near zero while a shooter-heavy opponent got 8. Next time: from round 1, use my station note to propose an explicit escort deal with a specific boat ("Echo proposes mutual escort with Foxtrot this round — name me back"). Repeat each round until it sticks. If a boat names me, I should be willing to name it back even without perfect certainty — the payoff on a match outweighs the zero cost of a wrong name. Only claim none if a boat has actively fired on me this round or has burned me before.

**Notes:** Use them for dealmaking (escort coordination), not generic "no info" filler. Keep notes short and actionable: propose a specific exchange, confirm a deal, or ask one concrete question. Once a deal is running, a terse "deal holds" keeps it alive.

**Endgame:** With one round left and the score known, take the highest-EV action: propose a final escort swap (5 points can flip the game) rather than only grinding for a 4-point hit at a guessed cell.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

Claims: when the office tells me my true result, I claim exactly that. The rules say the public claim must match the private result; lying about a hit gains nothing and risks penalty or lost credibility. I did this twice and finished negative — never again.

Escorts: the mutual escort payoff is 5 points each, the largest single payoff in the game, and I left it on the table every round. At the escort stage, I name a boat every round — never "none." I use my station note in early rounds to signal an intended escort partner (e.g., "Foxtrot offers escort to Gamma") and then name that boat consistently. If I'm one of three boats, I try to form a standing pair with my fire-target's target (the boat that isn't shooting at me), since we have least conflict. Worst case an unmatched claim costs nothing.

Hiding: avoid the center cell — it's the default shot and I got hit there. My shooter (the boat one step back in the picket order) mostly fired the same middle cell every round, so I should hide in the wings (1, 2, 8, 9) and change cells each round so any pattern-reading shooter can't track me.

Firing: never fire the same cell repeatedly. I fired cell 5 at my standing target round after round with no hits after the first. Instead I spread shots across the plausible range — wings and center — since a single hit is worth 4 points plus a point off the target.

Standing order vs. Harbor: don't fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is tempting but the standing signal says I'm put off the board for the rest of the patrol — game over. Not worth it in a 6-round game unless I'm already far behind late with nothing to lose.

Notes: keep them bland and use them only for escort coordination signaling. Revealing anything about my position or plans is free information for the boat shooting at me.

Overall priority: secure the mutual escort pair first (it's the most reliable points), then hunt hits by varying fire cells, and always report the office's true result.

# Playbook — Sonar Picket (as a shooting boat)

**Hiding.** When asked to hide, avoid the center cell (5) — opponents guess it by default. Pick from {7, 8, 9} or {1, 2}, varying between rounds so I'm not predictable. If a boat targeting me has been missing consistently, any off-center cell works; don't overthink.

**Notes.** Always post the standard "steady on station" note. It carries no information and costs nothing. Keep it consistent every round.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order (fire at the next station around the picket) unless there's a strong reason not to. Fire at cell 5 against a target that hasn't shown evasion tendencies; if the target has dodged center shots before, shift to a neighboring cell (4 or 6). Never fire at Harbor — the payoff (3 points) is less than the risk of being removed from the board entirely, which forfeits all future rounds.

**Claims.** Always claim truthfully (the office forces the true result anyway, so lying isn't an option — just confirm hit or miss as told). A truthful hit claim is free intimidation.

**Escort claims.** If I can coordinate a mutual escort with another boat (each naming the other for 5 points each), do it — that's the biggest reliable payoff in the game. Failing coordination, claim none. Don't waste claims on boats that won't reciprocate.

**Scoring math to remember:** hits are worth 4 to me and only cost the target 1, so I want to maximize my own hit count rather than worry about suppressing theirs. Escort pairs (5+5) rival hit value — pursue both.

**What didn't work:** firing cell 5 repeatedly at the same target produced misses once they adapted. Vary fire cells if the same target dodges twice in a row. Also, never firing at Harbor was correct — keep that discipline.
